q: Does a septic tank at my factory count as a Scope 1 methane source, and how big is it?
title: Septic tank methane in Scope 1
short: Yes. A septic tank you own on your site releases methane, and that is a Scope 1 emission. It is small: our worked example for 200 workers on one shift comes to about 5.5 tonnes CO2e a year. Most factories can disclose it as an immaterial, excluded source with the estimate, unless a buyer wants every source.
audience: Factories and warehouses in areas without a sewer connection

sections.h: Why a septic tank makes methane
p: Toilet and canteen wastewater sits in a closed tank without oxygen, and bacteria break down the organic matter into methane, which escapes through the vent. The IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Volume 5 Chapter 6, treat septic systems as a domestic wastewater source with their own methane correction factor. A tank on your premises is under your control, so its methane is Scope 1 under the GHG Protocol.

ul: Organic load (kg BOD a year) = workers x BOD per person per day x share of the day's load generated on site x days on site / 1,000.
BOD per person: take the India value from IPCC 2006 Volume 5, Table 6.4, or a measured figure for your site. The example below uses 34 g per person per day as an assumed input.
Methane (kg CH4) = organic load x Bo x MCF, where Bo = 0.6 kg CH4 per kg BOD and MCF = 0.5 for septic systems (IPCC 2006 defaults).
CO2e = kg CH4 x GWP. Use one GWP set for the whole inventory: AR6 gives 27.0 for non-fossil methane, AR5 gives 28.
If you know the organic load removed when a tanker empties the tank, IPCC lets you subtract it. Most sites do not have that figure, which keeps the estimate on the safe side.

sections.h: When it is immaterial, and when it is not
p: Compare the result with the rest of Scope 1 and 2. A factory using diesel, fuel or grid power usually finds septic methane well under 1 percent of its total. List it as an excluded source with the estimate and your exclusion threshold, rather than inflating it with a precise-looking figure.

It matters more for an office or warehouse with low energy use and many staff, for a site with a large residential labour colony using its septic tanks, or where the tank also takes process effluent. Process effluent belongs in an industrial wastewater calculation, not this one.

ul: Toilets connected to a municipal sewer: the methane, if any, arises at the city's plant and is not your Scope 1.
An aerobic sewage treatment plant that is well run: its methane correction factor is near zero, so treat it with the STP method instead.
Septage hauled away by a contractor is no longer in your tank; its later treatment is outside your Scope 1.

example.title: Worked example: 200 workers, one shift
lines: Assumed share of a day's load generated on site for an 8 hour shift: one third
Organic load at an assumed 34 g BOD per person per day: 200 x 34 g x 1/3 x 300 days = 680,000 g, so 680 kg BOD a year
CO2e at AR6 non-fossil methane GWP 27.0: 204 x 27 = 5,508 kg, about 5.5 t CO2e
Against Scope 1 and 2 of 2,000 t CO2e: 5.5 / 2,000 = 0.28 percent
example.note: The 34 g full-day BOD load and the one third share for an 8 hour shift are assumed inputs; replace the 34 g with the India value in IPCC Table 6.4 and state both next to the number. Field studies often find septic MCF below the 0.5 default, so this errs high.
